content.title: Texas men’s basketball coach Sean Miller tackles reloading Longhorns for 2025-26 season
content.text: Although it’s not his first time taking over a program, the rules in college sports have certainly changed since new Texas head coach Sean Miller last had to build a program. It’s been an uphill road just four months into his tenure on the Forty Acres, convincing pieces of last year’s corps to return while bolstering talent in the portal and high school. But it looks like the “drinking out of a water hose” period for both Miller and the Longhorns has started to come to an end, giving a good idea of the opening night roster. “I’ve been really not surprised at all, but very, very happy with the progress that we’ve made as a group,” Miller said. “The number of players that will be on this year’s team have a lot of history and experience in college basketball. I think that’s still a really powerful force when it comes to America’s best teams in college basketball.” The Texas men’s basketball head coaching gig is not the easiest job on the Forty Acres. It arguably has the shortest leash, with Miller becoming the program’s fourth head coach in the past decade. Couple that with the fact that men’s basketball is objectively the hardest to recruit and retain. That was true before the age of Name, Image and Likeness (NIL) and the transfer portal — it’s only gotten harder. Miller emphasised the retention of their most experienced players, fostering talent instead of renting it for a “cup of coffee.” Throwing out the example of reigning national champion, Florida, Miller noted the Gators for having an amazing formula for recruiting. “My first year at Xavier, we played Florida in Portland and they had a couple of young players that were freshmen … two and a half years later and there they are as an older upperclassman in year three in their program,” Miller said. Although it’s been less than half a year into his tenure, finding the right formula in balancing high school, international and portal recruiting is crucial to Miller this offseason and into the future. “My hope is less turnover when it comes to those that you want to come back,” Miller said. “Fortunately or unfortunately, (the players) have unlimited choices and they can move quickly.” Boosting Miller’s philosophy in year one, he was able to retain 2024 starters senior guard Jordan Pope and graduate guard Tramon Mark, along with explosive talent senior guard Chendall Weaver, who was sidelined the majority of last season with a hip injury before coming back late in the season. “Tramon and Jordan, they not only have experience in college basketball, but I think there’s real value and experience here when you return,” Miller said. Miller had tremendous praise for Weaver, suggesting that if he had not gotten injured, the Longhorns’ season could have been drastically different. “I think if Chendall didn’t get injured a year ago, I think the total wins in terms of Texas would have been great,” Miller said. “Chendall impacts the game in so many ways.” Despite holding out the hope of being ready from the jump, Miller is taking into account any possible growing pains that come with a coaching regime change, especially with a 60 percent turnover rate from last season’s squad. “I think it’s going to take a little time to put it all together,” Miller said. “New staff, new terminology, new program for players that weren’t really a part of our summer program. My hope is that you see us get better each week.” Possibly making the system transition easier on the court and in the locker room, Miller was able to bring former Xavier forwards graduate Lassina Traore and junior guard/forward Dailyn Swain, who are familiar with his system. Additionally, the Longhorns were able to acquire impactful upperclassmen in the portal, such as guard Simeon Wilcher and forward Camden Heide, bolstering the experience Miller is looking for. Texas opens the Sean Miller era Nov. 4, facing off against perennial college basketball power, the Duke Blue Devils, at the Spectrum Center in Charlotte, North Carolina. About the Contributor Nicholas is a journalism major from San Antonio, Texas. He got his start at UTSA’s student newspaper, The Paisano, covering UTSA football and the UFL’s San Antonio Brahmas. Since transferring to UT, he has covered Texas Football, Texas Men’s Basketball, Texas Baseball, Round Rock Express and Austin Spurs. Outside of Daily Texan, Nicholas is a staff writer at 100 Degree Hockey covering the Texas Stars and is a contributor at Longhorns on SI.
